label: Stress
title: Bhagavad Gita on Stress: 7 Verses for Heavy Days
description: Seven verses for when everything feels like too much, from Krishna's first lesson on what passes (2.14) to working with the fever gone (3.30). Sanskrit, plain English and one thing to try.
h1: Bhagavad Gita on stress: 7 verses for heavy days
subtitle: For the inbox, the deadline and the knot in your shoulders. Read one a day, or all seven on your next break.
keywords: bhagavad gita shlokas to calm the mind
bhagavad gita on pressure at work
intro: The Gita is spoken minutes before a war, to a man whose hands are shaking. Krishna knew what pressure does to a mind. These seven verses start with his first lesson, that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. Then come two pictures of steadiness, a lotus leaf and the ocean, and two practical verses on balance and on working with the fever gone. The last is from the Yoga Vasishtha, about a king who found freedom and kept his job.

days.heading: This will pass, and you can bear it
days.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
days.forYou: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.
days.today: Write down what's pressing on you. Next to each one, write roughly when it will be over.
days.note: This is about the ordinary ups and downs of life. If someone is harming or mistreating you, act on it.

days.heading: Why stress steals happiness
days.line: Without inner discipline there's no clarity; without clarity, no peace; and without peace, where is happiness?
days.forYou: Krishna lays out a chain. An unsettled mind has no clarity, without clarity there is no peace, and without peace there is no happiness, however good things look on paper. The workload is one part of stress. The other part is a mind with no place to stand.
days.today: Notice where your mind is during the busiest hour today: on the task, or three tasks ahead?

days.heading: Like a lotus leaf
days.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
days.forYou: A lotus leaf sits in water all its life, and the water still beads and rolls off it. Krishna uses it for someone who works fully and lets the mess around them roll off. You stay in the pond and keep your surface dry.
days.today: After your hardest conversation today, take one breath and picture the water rolling off.

days.heading: The ocean doesn't overflow
days.line: Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and still. Let demands enter you the same way.
days.forYou: Rivers keep pouring into the ocean and it stays full and still. Demands will keep coming. In Krishna's picture, peace comes from being deep enough to take them in.
days.today: When a new request lands, pause before replying. Let it arrive before you react.

days.heading: Eat, rest, work, sleep: in measure
days.line: Moderate in food and rest, in work and play, in sleep and waking: that's how sorrow eases.
days.forYou: This is the Gita at its most practical. Krishna tells Arjuna that the yoga which ends sorrow belongs to someone moderate in food, movement, work, sleep and waking. A lot of stress starts as a schedule with no rest built into it.
days.today: Pick one thing to put back in balance this week: a proper meal, a fixed bedtime, or a real break.

days.heading: Act with the fever gone
days.line: Hand your work to something higher, drop the 'mine' and the hoping, and act with the fever gone.
days.forYou: The Sanskrit is vigata-jvaraḥ: with the fever gone. Krishna still wants Arjuna to fight, and to fight without the heat of 'mine' and anxious hoping. Offer the work to something larger than your worry, and do it.
days.today: Before your next big task, say what it's for beyond you. Then begin.
days.note: Surrender here means letting go of anxious grasping. Your judgement and responsibility stay with you.

days.heading: A king who didn't leave his job

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.body: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.forYou: When stress builds, it's tempting to dream of quitting everything. Janaka kept the same work and held it differently.
days.today: Do one task today the way Janaka would: fully, and without checking for applause.

verse.sanskrit: शीघ्रमुत्तिष्ठ भद्रं ते नियतं कार्यमाचर । न कालमतिवर्तन्ते महान्तः स्वेषु कर्मसु ॥
verse.line: Get up and do today's work. Great people don't let the hour slip by.

faq.q: What does the Bhagavad Gita say about stress?
faq.a: Krishna's first teaching (2.14) is that pleasure and pain, heat and cold come and go, and can be borne. Later he describes the steady person as a lotus leaf untouched by water (5.10) and an ocean that rivers can't overflow (2.70), and he recommends balance in food, work, rest and sleep (6.17).

faq.q: Which Gita shloka calms the mind?
faq.a: 2.14 (mātrā-sparśās tu kaunteya) is the one Krishna uses first. 2.70, the ocean that stays still as rivers pour in, and 6.19, the lamp in a windless place, are also widely read for calm.

faq.q: Is the Gita telling me to just accept a stressful situation?
faq.a: No. The Gita is spoken to someone about to act. It asks you to bear what passes and act without anxious grasping. If a situation is harming you, changing it is part of acting well.
